message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection, Thornbury District Council

## Overall verdict

The pilot is a good foundation, and the cost arithmetic in Table 2 is correct. But the conclusions in the summary and the recommendation don't follow from the data:

1. **Participation was not similar across housing types.** Houses reached 66% and flats 21%, so the case for a single uniform service is contradicted by the study's own table.
2. **The projection uses a 64% participation rate that doesn't appear anywhere in the pilot data.** The pilot figure is 57%. Corrected, tonnage falls by about 13%.
3. **Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year**, well below either projection, so the disposal saving and the claim that treatment is local both fail for a large share of the tonnage.
4. **With corrected tonnage, the net cost already exceeds the £520,000 allocation**, before the capacity problem or any missing costs are counted.

## Major issues

### 1. Flats participated at a third of the rate of houses

Table 1's own figures (the arithmetic checks out):

| Housing type | Participation | Yield per participating household |
|---|---|---|
| Houses | 66% | 1.9 kg/week |
| Flats | **21%** | 1.4 kg/week |
| All | 57% | 1.9 kg/week (more precisely 1.86) |

The text says participation was "broadly similar across housing types." It wasn't: flats participated at under a third of the rate of houses. This is common, because flats often lack outdoor space for caddies, have communal bin stores and see more resident turnover. The data point toward a **tailored approach for flats**, such as communal food bins, bin-store signage and work with managing agents. They don't support one uniform service. About 10,400 of the district's households are flats, so this matters.

### 2. The projection uses the wrong participation rate

Section 3 applies a "64% participation rate." The pilot's overall rate was **57%**, and houses alone were 66%. 64% matches neither. The pilot's mix of 20% flats is the same as the district's, so 57% is directly applicable.

| Basis | Calculation | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|
| As stated (64%, 1.9 kg) | 52,000 × 64% × 1.9 kg × 52 | ~3,290 |
| Pilot overall (57%, 1.86 kg) | 52,000 × 57% × 1.86 kg × 52 | ~2,870 |
| By housing type | Houses ~2,710 + flats ~160 | **~2,870** |

So the realistic projection is about **2,870 tonnes**, roughly 420 tonnes (13%) lower.

Two further cautions about using the pilot figures:
- Six-month pilots often show a novelty effect, with participation falling once the service becomes routine.
- January to June doesn't cover the full seasonal pattern.

A lower sensitivity case would be sensible.

### 3. Brookfield cannot take the projected tonnage

Brookfield offers **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. That's well short of either projection:

- Using the paper's figure, about **1,490 tonnes** a year is over capacity.
- Using the corrected figure, about **1,070 tonnes** is over capacity.

The paper doesn't say where the excess would go.
- **The 46-mile plant** has an unknown gate fee, plus much higher haulage cost and vehicle time.
- **Incineration** would wipe out the saving on those tonnes. Collecting food waste separately only to burn it would also undermine the purpose of the service and could breach the separate-collection requirement.

The author's summary says "treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away." That's true for only about 55–63% of the projected tonnage.

### 4. The funding claim doesn't hold once the corrections are made

The paper's cost arithmetic is correct: vehicles £141,400, crews £408,000, total £733,400.

| | Disposal saving | Net cost | vs £520k allocation |
|---|---|---|---|
| As stated (3,290 t, all at Brookfield) | £243,000 | £490,400 | Covered |
| Corrected tonnage (2,870 t, all at Brookfield) | ~£212,500 | **~£520,900** | **Not covered** |
| Corrected tonnage, Brookfield capped at 1,800 t | ≤ £133,200 on Brookfield tonnes; remainder uncertain or negative | **~£600,000+** | **Not covered** |

On top of this:
- The allocation is described as **"provisional"** and the Government has only "indicated" funding. The paper calls the service "fully funded," which overstates the certainty. It also doesn't say how long the funding lasts.
- **The cost table is not complete**, despite "every cost line is shown." Missing or unclear items:
  - a spare vehicle (with six vehicles and none spare, one breakdown means missed rounds)
  - cover for crew holiday and sickness
  - whether the £34,000 includes employer NI and pension
  - supervision and management
  - the dedicated phone line and web staffing
  - haulage to the treatment site, if the vehicles don't tip there directly
  - financing cost on the £990,000 of vehicles
  - disposal of rejected contaminants

## Other issues

**Timetable.** Ordering vehicles in December for delivery in March assumes a three-month lead time. Specialist collection vehicles often take considerably longer. This is the critical path, and the paper should:
- confirm the lead time in writing with the supplier
- explain what happens if the vehicles arrive late, given that crew training and caddy delivery are also planned for March

**Statutory deadline.** Under the Simpler Recycling reforms, the deadline for weekly household food waste collections in England was 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some councils. The paper should say whether Thornbury has such an arrangement, because an April 2027 start may otherwise already be late.

**Evidence presented without data.**
- The 81% satisfaction figure comes from "surveyed pilot households." The paper should give the response rate and say whether non-participants were included, since participants are more likely to reply and more likely to be positive.
- The "consistent yields" and the steady fall in missed collections are stated without any weekly figures. A trend chart would support both claims, or show if they don't hold.

**Contamination.** Under 2% is a good result, but it comes from spot checks during a novelty period. It's worth monitoring after roll-out.

## Suggested changes before Cabinet

1. **Correct the participation rate** to 57%, or model houses and flats separately. Restate tonnage at about 2,870 t, with a lower sensitivity case.
2. **Replace the "uniform service" conclusion** with a costed approach for flats.
3. **Set out a treatment plan for the tonnage over 1,800 t**, with costs, or negotiate more capacity at Brookfield before committing.
4. **Rebuild the financial table:**
   - add the missing cost lines
   - use the corrected tonnage and treatment costs
   - present the funding as provisional, showing the gap if it falls short
5. **Confirm the vehicle lead time** and add a contingency plan for late delivery.
6. **Clarify the council's position against the statutory deadline.**

The pilot gives Thornbury useful local evidence. Read correctly, though, it shows the service is **not** fully funded as designed, can't be fully treated locally until 2029, and needs a different approach for flats. Cabinet should see those points before it approves the roll-out and the vehicle order.
